title: What is a functional interface (SAM interface), what are examples from java.util.function, how does @FunctionalInterface help, is it mandatory, can a FI extend another interface, and can it have default and static methods?

s1_definition.profdef: A functional interface has exactly ONE abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). It can have ANY number of `default` methods (with body) and `static` methods — only the abstract method count matters. `@FunctionalInterface` is OPTIONAL but strongly recommended: it makes the compiler verify that exactly one abstract method exists — accidentally adding a second causes a compile error. A functional interface CAN extend another interface as long as the resulting interface still has exactly one abstract method. Core interfaces in `java.util.function`: `Predicate<T>` (T to boolean — filtering), `Function<T,R>` (T to R — transformation), `Consumer<T>` (T to void — side effects), `Supplier<T>` (nothing to T — factory/lazy creation), `BiFunction<T,U,R>`, `UnaryOperator<T>` (extends Function, same input/output type), `BinaryOperator<T>` (extends BiFunction, all same type — used in reduce).
s1_definition.analogy: A functional interface is like a bank form with exactly ONE blank to fill in: the Predicate form has "Is this trade valid? YES/NO." The Function form has "Convert this trade to a receipt." The Consumer form has "Process this trade (no response needed)." The Supplier form has "Generate a new trade ID." You can add instructions (default methods) and stamps (static methods) to the form — but there is only ONE blank for the customer to fill in. `@FunctionalInterface` is the quality control stamp that says "I verify this form has exactly one blank."
s1_definition.oneliner: Functional interface = ONE abstract method. @FunctionalInterface = compile-time guard. Can have unlimited default + static methods. Predicate/Function/Consumer/Supplier are the four pillars.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A functional interface has exactly ONE abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). It can have ANY number of `default` methods (with body) and `static` methods — only the abstract method count matters. `@FunctionalInterface` is OPTIONAL but strongly recommended: it makes the compiler verify that exactly one abstract method exists — accidentally adding a second causes a compile error. A functional interface CAN extend another interface as long as the resulting interface still has exactly one abstract method. Core interfaces in `java.util.function`: `Predicate<T>` (T to boolean — filtering), `Function<T,R>` (T to R — transformation), `Consumer<T>` (T to void — side effects), `Supplier<T>` (nothing to T — factory/lazy creation), `BiFunction<T,U,R>`, `UnaryOperator<T>` (extends Function, same input/output type), `BinaryOperator<T>` (extends BiFunction, all same type — used in reduce).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A functional interface is like a bank form with exactly ONE blank to fill in: the Predicate form has "Is this trade valid? YES/NO." The Function form has "Convert this trade to a receipt." The Consumer form has "Process this trade (no response needed)." The Supplier form has "Generate a new trade ID." You can add instructions (default methods) and stamps (static methods) to the form — but there is only ONE blank for the customer to fill in. `@FunctionalInterface` is the quality control stamp that says "I verify this form has exactly one blank."

**One line to remember:** Functional interface = ONE abstract method. @FunctionalInterface = compile-time guard. Can have unlimited default + static methods. Predicate/Function/Consumer/Supplier are the four pillars.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank's trade validation system has 15 different validation rules scattered across the codebase as separate classes.** Each class implements a `TradeValidator` interface with a `validate` method. Adding a new rule requires creating a new class file. The team refactors to use functional interfaces: each rule becomes a lambda or method reference, rules compose with `.and()` and `.or()`, and common rules are shared as static factory methods.

**What the project will show:** Custom @FunctionalInterface with default composition methods (and, or, negate), static factory methods for common validators, all 7 core functional interfaces used in a trade processing pipeline, and a validation engine that composes rules dynamically.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Request: validate TRD-003. EntityManager loads the trade from PostgreSQL.

**Step 2.** The composed validator is built: `hasAccountId().and(hasSymbol()).and(hasPositiveQuantity()).and(validSide()).and(maxAmount(10M))`. This is a CHAIN of 5 TradeValidator lambdas connected by `.and()` default methods.

**Step 3.** `composedRule.validate(trade)` executes: hasAccountId checks trade.getAccountId() — it is BLANK → returns false. Because of `.and()` short-circuit, the entire chain returns false immediately.

**Step 4.** Individual rules are checked for error messages: each validator in the Map is tested independently. "accountId required" fails. Others pass. Failures list: ["accountId required"].

**Step 5.** Response returned: `{valid: false, failedRules: ["accountId required"]}`.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ @FunctionalInterface ANATOMY ═══

  @FunctionalInterface
  interface TradeValidator {
      boolean validate(Trade trade);                    // 1 ABSTRACT — lambdas implement THIS

      default TradeValidator and(TradeValidator other);  // DEFAULT — does NOT count
      default TradeValidator or(TradeValidator other);   // DEFAULT — does NOT count
      default TradeValidator negate();                   // DEFAULT — does NOT count

      static TradeValidator hasAccountId();              // STATIC — does NOT count
      static TradeValidator hasSymbol();                 // STATIC — does NOT count
  }
  // Total abstract: 1. Total default: 3. Total static: 2. VALID functional interface (Recommended) 

  ═══ COMPOSITION ═══

  TradeValidator composed = hasAccountId()     // rule 1
      .and(hasSymbol())                         // rule 1 AND rule 2
      .and(hasPositiveQuantity())               // ... AND rule 3
      .and(validSide())                         // ... AND rule 4
      .and(maxAmount(10M));                     // ... AND rule 5

  composed.validate(trade):
    hasAccountId? → "" → FALSE → short-circuit → return FALSE
    (hasSymbol, hasPositiveQuantity, validSide, maxAmount NEVER CALLED — short-circuit!)

  ═══ 7 CORE FUNCTIONAL INTERFACES IN PIPELINE ═══

  Predicate<Trade>:         trade -> trade.isActive()          → stream.filter()
  Function<Trade,BigDecimal>: Trade::getAmount                 → stream.map()
  Consumer<Trade>:          trade -> log.info(trade.id())      → stream.forEach()
  Supplier<String>:         () -> UUID.randomUUID().toString() → Optional.orElseGet()
  UnaryOperator<BigDecimal>: amount -> amount * taxRate        → List.replaceAll()
  BinaryOperator<BigDecimal>: BigDecimal::add                  → stream.reduce()
  BiFunction<Trade,BigDecimal,Trade>: (trade, fee) -> withFee  → Map.compute()
```
sections.s5c_hld:
**What is HLD?** The system-wide view. Here functional interfaces (the SAM concept and the core java.util.function family) are the glue that lets a loan-decisioning platform accept pluggable behavior as lambdas.

```
  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    HLD — Loan Decision Platform (functional interfaces as behavior plugs)
  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ┌─────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
  │ Loan Portal │  │ Mobile App   │  │ Partner API  │  ← Client Layer
  └──────┬──────┘  └──────┬───────┘  └──────┬───────┘
         └────────────────┼─────────────────┘ HTTPS
                          ▼
                ┌──────────────────────┐
                │    API Gateway       │  ← JWT, rate limit
                └──────────┬───────────┘
                           ▼
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  LoanDecisionService (×4)                 │  ← Application Layer
         │  Predicate<Applicant>  eligibility SAM    │
         │  Function<Applicant,Score> scoring SAM    │
         │  BiFunction<Score,Policy,Decision>        │
         │  Consumer<Decision> notify SAM            │
         └──────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                JDBC │
                     ▼
         ┌──────────────────┐
         │ PostgreSQL       │  ← applicants, decisions
         └──────────┬───────┘
                    │ replication
                    ▼
         ┌──────────────────┐
         │ Read Replica (×2)│  ← risk reports
         └──────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Redis: policy cache; Observability: Prom/ELK/Jaeger│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The HLD insight: each decision stage is expressed through a core functional interface. Because each is a Single Abstract Method type, the platform injects behavior as lambdas or method references, keeping the service skeleton fixed while the actual rules vary per product.
sections.s5d_lld:
**What is LLD?** Zoom into LoanDecisionService to show the SAM structure and how the core java.util.function interfaces slot in as fields.

```
  ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
       LLD — Functional Interfaces & SAM (FAANG Level)
  ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Strategy (SAM): each functional interface = a swappable strategy │
  │  Pipeline: Function.andThen chains scoring → decision             │
  │  Factory: Function.identity() / Predicate.not() built-ins         │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: each SAM does one thing (test, score, decide, notify)         │
  │  O: new product = new lambdas, service code unchanged             │
  │  L: any Predicate<Applicant> substitutes for another             │
  │  I: Predicate/Function/Consumer are tiny single-method contracts  │
  │  D: service depends on functional-interface types, not concretes  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Core java.util.function family (SAM each) ─────────────
   Predicate<T>      test(T): boolean        eligibility
   Function<T,R>     apply(T): R             scoring
   BiFunction<T,U,R> apply(T,U): R           decision from score+policy
   Supplier<T>       get(): T                reference-id generator
   Consumer<T>       accept(T): void         notification sink
   UnaryOperator<T>  apply(T): T             normalize applicant data

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           LoanDecisionService                 │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  - eligible: Predicate<Applicant>             │  SAM: test
  │  - score:    Function<Applicant, Score>       │  SAM: apply
  │  - decide:   BiFunction<Score,Policy,Decision>│  SAM: apply
  │  - notify:   Consumer<Decision>               │  SAM: accept
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + process(a: Applicant): Decision            │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. service.process(applicant Priya CUR3001)
  2.   → if (!eligible.test(applicant)) return REJECTED   Predicate SAM
  3.   → Score s = score.apply(applicant)                 Function SAM
  4.   → Decision d = decide.apply(s, policy)             BiFunction SAM
  5.   → notify.accept(d)                                 Consumer SAM
  6.   → return d  (APPROVED, limit Rs.250,000, BigDecimal)
```

The LLD makes the SAM idea concrete: every functional interface has exactly one abstract method, which is why the compiler can accept a lambda or method reference in its place. The `@FunctionalInterface` annotation documents intent and makes the compiler enforce the single-method rule, while the core `java.util.function` interfaces cover the common shapes so teams rarely need to define their own.
sections.s6_takeaway:
A functional interface has exactly one abstract method. The FunctionalInterface annotation is optional but recommended as a compile-time guard that prevents accidentally adding a second abstract method. Default methods and static methods do not count toward the abstract method limit — they have implementations. This means a functional interface like Predicate can have one abstract method (test) plus three default methods (and, or, negate) plus one static method (not) and still be a valid functional interface that lambdas can implement.

In my trade validation engine, I created a custom TradeValidator functional interface with one abstract method (validate), three default composition methods (and, or, negate), and five static factory methods (hasAccountId, hasSymbol, hasPositiveQuantity, validSide, maxAmount). Each factory returns a lambda implementing the validate method. The composition methods return new lambdas that chain the original validators. This replaces 15 separate validator classes with 15 one-line lambdas that compose fluently: `hasAccountId().and(hasSymbol()).and(maxAmount(10M))`. Adding a new validation rule means adding one static factory method — no new class file, no modification to existing code.

The seven core functional interfaces in java.util.function cover all common function signatures: Predicate for boolean results used in filtering, Function for transformation used in mapping, Consumer for side effects used in forEach, Supplier for lazy value creation used in orElseGet, UnaryOperator for same-type transformation used in replaceAll, BinaryOperator for same-type reduction used in reduce, and BiFunction for two-argument functions used in Map.compute. These compose with methods like andThen, compose, and, or, and negate — enabling complex behavior from simple building blocks without creating intermediate classes.
